opus-5.5.text:
I think traditional control theory and system modeling are still enormously valuable, and in a way their value has become clearer as reinforcement learning has matured.

When I first got into RL, there was this almost romantic idea that you could throw away all the structure, give the agent a reward, and let it learn everything from scratch. That works in some settings like games or simulation, where data is essentially free and failure has no cost. But once you move to real physical systems, like robots, vehicles, or anything that interacts with the real world, you quickly run into the limits of pure model-free learning. Sample efficiency becomes a huge problem, safety becomes a huge problem, and you start to really appreciate what decades of control theory have given us.

There are a few places where I see that value most clearly.

The first is **structure and priors**. A good system model, even an approximate one, tells you a lot about how the world behaves: the dynamics, the constraints, what's physically possible. If you bake that into learning, through model-based RL, residual learning on top of a nominal controller, or physics-informed models, you need far less data and you generalize better. You're not asking the agent to rediscover Newton's laws.

The second is **stability and safety guarantees**. Control theory has a rich vocabulary for reasoning about stability, robustness, and constraint satisfaction: Lyapunov functions, control barrier functions, robust and model predictive control. Pure RL policies are often black boxes; they may work well on average but give you no guarantee about the worst case. Combining learned components with these tools, like a safety filter around a learned policy, or using MPC as the backbone with learned costs or dynamics, is one of the most practical paths to deploying RL in the real world.

The third is **interpretability and debugging**. When something goes wrong in a system built on a clear model, you can ask *why*. You can look at the model error, the controller gains, the state estimates. With an end-to-end learned policy, failure analysis is much harder. Engineers who have to sign off on a system really care about that.

And the fourth is more conceptual. RL and optimal control are really two branches of the same tree. Bellman's work on dynamic programming sits at the root of both. Many ideas we celebrate in RL, like value functions, policy iteration, and trajectory optimization, have deep counterparts in control. So I think understanding control theory makes you a better RL researcher, because you can see what's genuinely new and what's being rediscovered.

That said, I don't think it's a one-way street. Learning brings things classical control struggles with: handling high-dimensional perception like raw images, dealing with dynamics too complex to model by hand, adapting to changing environments, and discovering strategies a human designer wouldn't think of. So to me, the most exciting work is at the intersection: using models where we have good knowledge, using learning where we don't, and using control-theoretic tools to keep the whole system reliable.

If I had to summarize it in one sentence: learning gives you flexibility, and control theory gives you trust. For real-world systems, you need both.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that control theory and system modeling haven't lost value in the RL era. If anything, they're the part of the field that keeps RL honest.

When I look at where RL actually works in the physical world, there's almost always a model-based or control-theoretic backbone underneath. The policy might be a neural network, but the simulator it was trained in was built from rigid-body dynamics. The reward shaping often encodes what a control engineer would call a cost function. The safety layer that keeps the robot from hurting itself is usually a constraint from classical control, not something the agent learned. So the "pure learning" story is a bit of a myth. We're almost always doing learning on top of structure.

The deeper reason is sample efficiency and guarantees. Model-free RL is extraordinarily data hungry, and real systems don't give you millions of trials. A good dynamics model, even an approximate one, collapses that problem enormously. You can plan, you can simulate, you can reason about what happens off the data distribution. And control theory gives you a vocabulary for things learning alone struggles with: stability, robustness to disturbances, what happens near the edge of the operating envelope. A learned policy can look great in the regime it was trained on and fail silently one step outside it. Lyapunov functions, reachability analysis, robust control, these are tools for reasoning about exactly that failure mode.

I'd also say the two fields are converging more than competing. Model-based RL is really just adaptive control with a different culture around it. Techniques like MPC with learned dynamics, or residual policies that learn a correction on top of a classical controller, are becoming the practical default for hard physical problems. The classical controller handles the easy, well-understood part of the problem, and learning handles the residual the model gets wrong, things like contact, friction, unmodeled compliance.

So the way I'd frame it: control theory tells you what you can guarantee and why, and RL tells you how to get good behavior where your model runs out. The interesting research is in the seam between those two, not in choosing one over the other. People who throw away the modeling tradition usually end up rediscovering it the hard way, one failed deployment at a time.

astra-6.text:
I think traditional control theory and system modeling are still very valuable, because reinforcement learning doesn’t make the underlying dynamics disappear. You still have a system with constraints, uncertainty, and limits on what you can observe or control.

Control theory gives us a way to reason about stability and robustness. Modeling helps us understand how our actions affect the system. Even an imperfect model can provide useful structure, so the learning algorithm doesn’t have to discover everything through trial and error. That matters especially on physical systems, where collecting data can be expensive and mistakes can damage hardware.

So I see these approaches as complementary. You might use a conventional controller for behavior you understand well, and reinforcement learning to compensate for effects that are difficult to model or to improve performance. The important question is how to combine the strengths of both: the structure and analysis of control theory with the flexibility of learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think traditional control theory and system modeling are still very valuable because reinforcement learning doesn’t remove the need to understand the system you’re controlling. You still have dynamics, constraints, uncertainty, and questions about stability.

If you have a useful model, you can use it to design a controller, generate training data, or give the learning algorithm a better starting point. Then reinforcement learning can help with the parts that are difficult to model, or optimize behavior beyond what a simplified model captures.

The important distinction is that getting a high reward in training is not the same as having a reliable controller. Control theory gives us tools to reason about stability and robustness, while modeling helps us understand where a learned policy might fail. So I see them as complementary. The goal is to use the structure we already understand and learn what we don’t.
